sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Okay now we were talking about the parts of the pig that you used when you started to tell me about the head.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: We cleaned some of the head meat and the liver and the heart and poil that and grind it and then what we'd trim off of the shoulders and the hams and then, and the other meat that use that we trimmed off of the pork shops and we'd grind that for sausage.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did you use the brains?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Yes we used the brains. The brains we generally kept out and fried them and eat them right away. We didn’t use them for anything else. And the leg we'd use, we'd boil, we'd clean them good and use them for souse, boil em.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did you throw the tail away?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: What's that?

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: I said did you throw the tail away?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Oh the most of it, it was just a stamp of the tail and some of the backbone we'd ah, we'd generally use that for Sauerkraut but then the neck, we called it the put, that made a good roast. You, you'd take pork chops off but the end would be a big piece that we'd roast and ah . . .

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: What about the ears?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Well we didn’t use ears. We threw them away (laughs)

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: And you used the tongue.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Yes the tongue. Sometimes we'd smoke the tongue, That would be good. We put it in salt grind and ah, and then smoke it when we'd smoke our, well we generally smoked them by themselves if we had a couple tongues. They would be good sliced cold after you boil them then after they're smoked and they're good fried, not fried, but just good when they're smoked then they're boiled, then they’re smoked and then you slice them and eat them cold.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: And all this needs was cooked outside over a fire?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: We generally, we had a butcher house where they had two iron kettles on the furnace, we called it a furnace and there we'd boil our ah, we rendered the lard you know in a kettle and ah, and we boiled the, the head meat and the liver and lungs, liver and heart and and that would get ground then for pudding.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: How did you keep some of the meat that you didn't smoke? Did you can it?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Only the sirloin. We canned the sirloin. And ah we fried that, we salted it in a crock and then let it set oh maybe just overnight and then we'd fry it and put it in jars and then boil up the, the frying, the pan where we, we'd take the meat out of the pan and then pour water in the pan and boil that up and put that water over the meat and then we'd screw our jars shut and put them in a cold water bath and bolt em for about fifteen minutes. That would seal em tight you know better than if we just sealed em after we fried em first and put them, we never had any trouble of not keeping them when we boiled them, a couple well about ten-fifteen minutes.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Then how did you prepare the meat for a meal?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Well then, it, it would be fried and they'd have the frying, the water where it was fried in that would be in the jar, we'd pour that all out and then put in, make the gravy over the meat.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: How often did you butcher?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: we did it twice in the winter, but then we'd butcher two at a time. (B) Okay, you were talking about tallow candles. You said that you also butchered a beef. How often did you do this just one beef a year?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Just one beef a year usually.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Was that a similar a process to the butchering of...

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: if we, if we could butcher beef at the same time then we'd put some of the odd fallings of the beef in with the, with the pork and grind it for sausage. And the, tallow we'd fry that out and we often sold tallow, we'd have a little bit of tallow we made tallow candles but not, not so many. Later on after we got the coal oil lights you know we didn't bother with tallow candles anymore. We just rendered the tallow and sold it or used it for a soap once in awhile we'd get some of that soap fat.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did you make other kinds of candles besides the tallow candle? You made the tallow candles in a mild, is that right.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Oh yes.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: What kind of wicking did you use? Something you brought or . . .

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: It, it was a special wicking that we'd buy at that time. I can’t just say what it was called, it was white, itwas, we would have two or three sticks which we generally put six candles in a mild at one time, and, and we'd put this twine the length that we’d want it, cut the length that we'd want it and put it over the, over the wooden sticks that we'd have and then run it down through the candle, through the mold and knot it at the other end, after we'd have six in the mold and have em inotted already then we'd pour the hot tallow over them and set them in a cold place till they got cold and then pull em out and they'd be tallow candles.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: How long did it take for them to harden.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Well it just depended how cold it was. If you'd set em out in the cold why they'd harden in a couple of hours. They'd be ready for use then and the candles we always had ah keep em at a cold place those that we wanted to use and we'd have special tallow candle holders where we'd put them in to light them.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: What was different about the tallow candle holder?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Well it, what we had were brass tallow candle holders we called them. They were, oh shaped a little like a small, like a smaller plate, shaped like a smallest pie plate and we'd have a snuffer would go with the candle holder and when the light would be burned up quite a bit why then you'd have to snuff it off and tallow candle holders, they would be nice if you tip them nice but what we had were brass and I'd scour them once a week we had to scour them and then they would look like old but it would tarnish them after they were used for about a week.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Do you remember what you had used to scour the holders?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Coal ashes. (J) Coal ashes.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Yes that's what we used to scour those. (3) Did you ever put a scent into you candle so that it would smell different than just the tallow?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: No not that I know of. I guess we didn't know that much yet (laughs)

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Was candle making a weekly chore or did you do it once for the whole year?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Well we just done that to, well if we kept tallow, why we could heat the tallow anytime and we made candles anytime of the year. But I, I don’t remember, we, we didn't use too many tallow candles then anymore. After I got older why then we used more different lights.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Do you remember the old brick bake ovens?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Yes. I remember them. My grandfather had a brick bake oven and they baked bread in it. They took so much wood in, they'd know just about what kind of wood they had to have and how much and they when that wood was all burned up they would have a scraper to scrape the ashes out and then they would have their bread ready to put in the oven. They'd put it all in at one time then while it was hot and ah they had to know how much wood to have and how hot the oven, but they had no thermometer or anything, you just had to judge that, you know at that time. Its ah, and I, I know that my aunt we never had any but I know that my aunt, I've seen her bake bread in the bake oven.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Where was that oven? Was it in her house or a separate building?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: no, it was definitely in a separate building. It had a roof over it, it was in a house and then they had the kind of wood that we needed we had that ready like a woodhouse you know we'd have it set up at the side like a bake oven. No bake oven bread, if the oven was just right, why it seemed we thought bake oven bread couldn’t be beat. We thought it was better than what we baked in our range.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did they take other things at the time they baked bread or did they just bake bread?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: It had to be a little hotter for pies and for cakes I think we backed cakes at the same time we baked bread but we generally had it a little hotter oven then when you baked pies. I don't think we put pies and cakes and bread all in at the same time.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: This Mrs. Hollenbach that you talked about who did the pow wowing and the, she was a midwife. Ah do you remember anything much about her? Did she ever tell anybody any of her secrets? How was pow-wowing passed from one person to another.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: I, I don't know whether she could teach anybody else or not. There was nobody else around that did pow-wowing that I know of. She was, she was brought, er they got her from oh sometimes from miles around they would fetch her well usually for a midwife. She seemed to know more about what, how to take care of it maybe or what to feed it first and she, and she was good for anybody that had pneumonia or inflammation of any kind. She pow-wowed for the information and she would make polise put polise on your chest to loosen it up. She had certain kinds of teas that she used to make polise. She tried to have seven different kinds of bitter teas she used ah I forget the name of the tea, of the tea that we used. And then she used I know what she used but I can't remember the names anymore of the different kinds of tea that she used but she gattered teas and roots out in the woods. She'd know just what to gather.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Was there ever any proof that she healed anybody or was it just whether you believed it or not?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Well I know that I had syphillis and all that I ever had done for it, she pow-wowed for it and it didn’t last long. My hand was swollen thick and (coughs) and she would pow-wow a couple times in a day. I'd have to stay there, she had, she has certain signs that she . . .

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: How much did she charge?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Oh she wouldn't charge anything. She would take whatever you'd give her. But she didn't want much but we always gave her something. But ah she, she didn’t charge. Oh for, for a confinement case she charged $2 and a half but then she would come a couple times then and after the first day till she seen that you was in good shape and alright.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Where did she live?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: She lived on a farm. I believe they call it Chesnet Ridge now I guess. Between Kratzerville and Shamakin Dam.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: What was her first name?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Rebecca Hollenbach

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Hollenbach?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Yes Rebecca Hollenbach.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: In addition to healing people do you know of any time could she put a hex on you? Did you know anybody who'd do that?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Oh I, I used to hear about that but oh she, she didn't do that. I know, I remember a lady she couldn’t, she couldn't or she was trying to bar the soap and she didn't get any soap it didn’t get strong, it wasn't ripe and then she said somebody bewitched her soap stuff that she couldn't bar soap and all, all her trouble was she hadn't put enough caustic soda in too make it strong. (laughs) Thats what I always thought. But ah I remember some people but I don't remember anybody that they blamed for bewitching but I, I heard people say about it, they'd say it was bewitched. (laughs)

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Do you remember some of the other cases? Was there any witchcraft in the area at all?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: No not that I not around where we lived.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did people ever tell stories of witchcraft or superstitions? You said your husbands mother had superstitions. What were they? Norman's Mother.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Yes. She was the one that said you couldn't go in swimming during dog days or you'd get boiled. And I don't know if there was anything else. Oh you couldn't change underwear between Christman and New Year.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Why was that?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: You, you’d get sick, you'd have to be washing all the year then.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did they ever have any proof that this came true?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab:
Oh well, one time my, my mother-in-law said that they, they got scarlet fever and she said they were sick so much from that time on all winter or all spring and after that they'd never would wash anymore between Christman and New Year (laughs) because they thought that was the reason. I don't know I guess there were some more things
but I just can't remember.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: You lived on a farm. How did, how did they do for instance harvesting of wheat before they had combines? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Oh yeah. They had a harvester that they used that they called a harvester and that would just there'd be a platform on the harvester and then every so often there would be a scraper come around and would scrape it off, just enough for one sheave. And then we'd have to have hired men come and tie up the, the tie up they wheat then on the sheave and you'd always have to have a couple of men to harvest you know it took men. Some to tie up the sheeves and some would tie er carry em together and put them on top and men at that time the couple first years after I was married we, the men just charged 50$ a day to harvest but you had to board them breakfast, dinner, and supper, but then later on they charged a dollar a day and then they didn't come for breakfast.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Were these local men or did they come from other area?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: No they were, they were men that had worked in the ore mines at that place called the Violet that wasn't more of a mile from our place and when the, the when the furnace shut down and they, they didn’t dig for ore anymore why then they had no work. Then they had to depend on working for the farmers.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Now that was the Winfield furnace that your talking about?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: And this ore mine, that was on the north side of the New Berlin Mountain.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Yes, Yes. Yes it wasn't so far from where our place, ah place where, there were places, there were a couple places on the mountain you know where you'd go down in the ore mines where they were working then. There were a good many working in there for pretty many years I guess. But when, when that shut down that they didn't, didn't run that furnace anymore why then of course those men were out of work.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Do you remember anything before the harvester came. Did you ever have to

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab:
Well they, the rye, rye wheat you'd cradle that, we called it cradeling, you didn't use a safe, you didn't use a safe to cut grass but we, we called it a credle to candle the rye and that you'd tie up at and you'd flale that out and use that rye
straw to make a, a string to tie the wheat. That was before they had bindertwine. They'd use rye straw to tie the wheat sheaves but then after later on then we had a binder, then it would, then we had bindertwine and then we would take and tie the sheaves but it would just tie sheaves and let that lay then the sheaves would have to be carried together and some man would stock them and then the wheat had to be loaded on wagons and hauled in the barn and mound into mound until we were ready for slashing. Then, then after it was slashed, but then the wheat would be run over a fanning mill to, it, it till it would be clean enough to sell or to use for to take to the mill. And a farming mill was just a, well you'd have your fanning mill on the slashing floor and you'd, you'd turn it by hand. Someone would put the wheat in and then maybe someone would have to shovel it away or it would run through the fanning mill and that wheat would be cleaned nice and clean though but it, it'd make alot of work. The whole winter (laughs) (3) What was the machine that was turned by horses?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Well we just called it the thrashing machine. It was older than, it was different I guess from the thrashing machines when they had those fraction ends that they would go around thrashing. They had a different machine then. That was later on then but that would clean it, clean the wheat better than would the old-fashioned thrashing machine where you use the horses to in place of steam heat.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: What, what job did the horses do?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab:
The, the horses would just go around in a ring. They’rd be a platform where the driver would stand in the middle of a platform and then there were arms going out to different places like the, like the arm of a tonque of a wagon. And then they’rd be usually about three to four horses and they would go around and that would keep the machine going to run the wheat to run the wheat through, to thrash it. But then even after they had the fraction and the different machine then we generally cleaned some of the wheat when we wanted it real clean to take to the mill for, we'd take our own wheat to the mill and have it ground for flour for bread. We always baked our own bread then. And then, but then to sell it sold why we didn’t have to run it all over
the farming mill, only what we wanted specially clean.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Do you remember anything about the ore mines that you mentioned earlier? Did you know anyone who worked in the ore mine?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Oh yes. The men that worked in the ore mine worked for us by the days then after they had no work anymore. They would work for us then oh help to make fences and, and in harvest you know to help, we would always have to have a couple men harvest.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did they ever talk about the mine?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Oh yes. Yes. Yes they were men that lived in a place we called Violet. There were a good many houses around just a little town. It was called the mining town. Then afterwards when they didn't work in the mines anymore the name was changed to Violet cause there were so many violets growing around there. But my, my father-in-law hauled ore to Winfield at that time there were different men around there that hauled ore and they had big heavy wagons and they'd have four horses in a wagon. It was heavy but they'd have it loaded pretty good. Then they'd haul, haul the ore to Winfield, we called it the furnace road, they'd go down the Furnace road to Winfield, that'd be kind of a bad road to Winfield.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Were the mines dangerous, were there ever any accidents or weren’t they similar to coal mines?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: No, no. No accidents happened. Not, not in the mining that I found out or anything but down at the furnace when they'd do the furnace I think they had some accidents. They had to do so much work you know when they built this, this furnace and smokestack and the buildings that they used at that time.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Do you have anything that you made notes of that you want to make sure that you tell me?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab:
No. I guess I just had about the wheat harvesting. You know after the hinder then they got these combines. Some people had the combines but it took a long time before everybody could have a combine because they were pretty expensive at first and some people thought you know they were too heavy to go in the field if it was a little
wet it would make the ground so hard and you had to let the wheat get so good and ripe because it would thrash it right away in the field you know you'd have a wagon coming after to put the wheat on bags and hauled it in or haul it to the mill or whereever you wanted to take it. Thrashing with a that was kind of a it was a big, big pole that you'd hold in you hand and then there was just a small pole at the end and then there was a hole dried in that ah the small flale would tie fast to the one that you'd hold and you'd just have that to, that would be oh well (laughs) I remember what they look like but I can't describe them. They ah...

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did you beat the wheat when you had it laying on the barn floor or did you...

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Yes we have the rye laying on the barn floor all in a row and then we'd go around with a flale to flale the grain out and then we'd tie up the straw or try not to break the straw too much because we wanted to use that to tie the wheat at each end. Take two bunches of rye straw and there was a way that they knew how to knot it together to make, make enough to tie em. That was before they had bindertwine.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did you ever make rag carpet?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: What?

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did you ever make rag carpet?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab:
Oh yes. All our clothes, our aprons or dresses or anything that we could tear them up in strips and then we had, had to sew carpet rags. We, we didn't like that (laughs) but we had so much work of sewing, sewing carpet rags and then we'd have enough to roll em on a ball then you’d have so many balls of carpet rags then you'd take em to the weavers and they would, they would weave em into carpet then. You had to buy the, well the different colored yarn to make the stripes in the carpet. Its been so long ago too that I don’t remember right but I well remember how we had to sew carpet rags and then take them to the weavers to make a new carpet. And brooms, we had alot of brooms we made still. We sold brown seed and ah and that would roll up in oh well the top of the stalk would be brushey and then you'd cut that off, it had to be a certain time, it, it just have to be when the time was just right to
cut it, just a certain time when it was ready to cut. Then we'd cut that off, cut the tops off of the brown corn and and take it to the, the what did they call the men that made the brooms. I forget (laughs)

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: The broommaker.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: (laughs) Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Do you remember how he made them.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Oh yes. I seen him make them. He had a machine to make them and, and I think we had wood that we had sawed to make broom handles too. Take the brown handles, we could sell broom handles you know at that time. I know oh we had alot of homemade brooms and they all always were good brooms.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Were they shaped like our brooms today?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Just like them?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: They were shaped just like the brooms that you get now. Maybe they were a little heavier. It's been so long you know I kinda forget about them.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: What about the quilting bees? Did you have many of those?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Oh, oh yes. We, we went to quilt-ins and that would be a great thing. Just the neighborhood around you know at that time we didn't, we walked quite alot where we went or drove in the horse and baggy or whatever we used what we had to drive with. We'd go to neighbors houses and they'd have, well we generally had about, oh generally about eight, four on each side of the quilt, to guilt and then when we'd have a quilt-in we'd always have a good dinner for, for the quilters and if some of them could stay later why we'd have dinner and supper for them. And but we, My mother and my sister and I quilted a good many quitts just quiltea them ourselves. We liked to guilt themselves better than to bother with having a quilt-in party.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Do you remember how old you were when you made your first guilt?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab:
Oh I was just eight years old when I made quilt patches. My mother always taught us to sew by hand. We were to learn to sew by hand good before we'd go on the sewing machine and she'd cut us patches, just, we'd called em nine patch, just, just
three in a row and then three rows and we'd sew them together to make a patch. Oh I remember how we used to make quilt patches. How we just started out with the nine point patch and we most always made our, our different quilts that we made, we most always made the patches by, sewed em by hand. We could sew em on the sewing machine but my mother thought they were nicer if they were sewed by hand. And ah, we made, we make quilts with the, with the, oh what do they call it when you saw it on top?

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Applicae

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Applicae. Yes. We have a big white patch about oh I'd say about 12" square and then we'd have a pattern to make a flower on it or a couple leaves or something and we'd applicae sew them on the quilt. They made nice quilts. I think my girls have some of them yet. I gave them to my girls so I don't have none anymore here but I have other quilts we, we . . .

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: How old would these quilts be then.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: My, my, my, my, my grandfather had got a whole spun quilt, he got it from home and when we were married they, he had got one from home that was homespun and she had got or my mother-in-law had got one from home and that was factory made though. It was, they were both nice. And she, she gave those quilts to my girls, the one that my father-in-law got from home my daughter Martha got and what my, my mother in-law got that my daughter Alice has and they would be, they would he over a hundred years old anyhow, quite a bit over a hundred because you know my, my father-in-law getting it from home and oh, oh, my daughter she thought that was a wonderful gift. And they never had used it at all they just kept it, you know, because they never use it and my daughter never used it more than she put it on the bed to see how it looked. (laughs) They’re expensive. A person could get a good price for them now if they'd want to sell them. SIDE TWO

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Do you remember what year New Berlin got electricity?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab:
Well lets see, (mumbled figuring in background) About 1904. Because the two first
years that I worked for Mrs. Lenker we, we just had coal oil lights and they had those big lights with round wicks in they made a nice light but there was no electricity in New Berlin at that time. But that was the two first years I lived there and I went there first in1902 and 1903 and in 1904, I think it was the third summer that I lived there that we got the electric and then there was no water either. You didn’t have indoor toilet because you had no water. And that, we just got water, oh just two years there yet after we had the toilet room. It must have been in about, well between 1904 and 1905 then when we got power and electricity in New Berlin. But before that you know we just had the street lights or the light with a pole on (laughs) or the pole with a light on and, and the man would come around and just put a certain amount of coal oil in and light it and then when that coal oil was all burned out then the light would go out itself and he was just supposed to put so much in then it was to last for several hours. That was until we got the electric.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did people go out at night?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Oh, well we, at that time, we always had church Sunday evenings. We, we'd go to church Sunday evenings and we'd have prayer meetings Wednesday evenings and then we'd have festivals in the town hall, & our church or Sunday School school would have icecream or cakes, different people baked cakes and we had a festival in the evenings but that was about all that was going on. There really was no, no factories at that time, not in New Berlin, there was nobody, the girls, alot of the girls used to go to Eagle Mere for I think it lasted for about eight weeks, they would go to these mountain resort and they would get good pay there. Alot of the young people would go to the,I know to Eagle Mere there was alot went, I don’t know and I can't name any other places I just remember that they went.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: You said about getting water in New Berlin and up until that time you didn’t have indoor plumbing. Can you remember the old outside plumbling?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: What, what we . . .

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Yeah, can you remember

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Well, well we'd, we just had well water and system water. We had a system. And a well. The well right outside of the kitchen door on the walk. And in the yard there was a, a system that the spounting run into that, that we had drainwater there that we used for washing. We had, there was no washing machines at that time. We had to wash everything by hand on the machine that you rubbed on.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: What about the outdoor bathrooms? You said that there was something very typical that they all were sort of the same on the inside. It was kind of funny to go to the bathroom.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Well people generally just hung pictures in the toilet. We, we would tack up old valentines of if we had nice calenders with nice pictures on why we'd, we'd hang them in and we used to have it all almost papered with something nice to look at.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: You said there was always a box full of newspapers there too.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: yes. (laughs) Yes, we didn't know anything about toilet paper at that time. We just had a box with newspapers in for on the toilet. And ah...

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: What about in the wintertime?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Well it was the same in the winter as in the summer only it was colder. It made no difference, why even the Slackers, they were very wealthy people, but no inside toilet as long as they didn't have the water.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: So when it snowed I guess it was pretty important to shove! a path to the . . .

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: (laughs) Yes. That was about the first thing they, they had to have a path shoveled to the, to the, we called them the out-houses at that time, they didn’t call them the bathroom because there was no bathroom (laughs)

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did you have sleighrides in the wintertime?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab:
Oh yes. We used to like when it snowed. Thats when we lived on the farm when we had a big shed and horses. We, we'd have someone that would, would drive, we’d we'd just have a, put straw in the, in the wagon box and, and you'd have boards for seats up along the side and there were, oh there were maybe a dozen or so go on a sleighride and we'd have a dance someplace or play playing parties. You know oft times you took
good to eat along and we'd make taffy sometimes and we’d have parties like that because we didn’t go too far, not like they go now in cars, because we had to drive or walk wherever we went then.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did you have traveling salesmen in those days?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Traveling salesmen. Oh yes, and I remember when peddlers used to come around, they'd have a pack on their back, I know when I was a kid I used to be afraid of the peddlers and they, they would come and they would have oh a variety of things in their pack and they'd always want to sell things. It seemed some of the jews had they said they got their start by peddling and, and they always were good managers or good workers it seemed because they usually started in the small scale and soon they'd start up a little store and they, they'd seem to prosper and get along alright. And I, I even know that they would matches, that they could come around with just big bundles of matches in that you could buy a box of matches that they were only you know like these penny boxes that they got now, they were bigger boxes but there'd be about six packs or boxes in a pack. They were larger matches. We often brought matches from him. And there would be so many we called them tramps that would go around and they'd come and ask for something to eat. They'd ask if they couldn't have a cup of coffee or whether they could have a, just anything that we could hand out, a piece of bread or pie or cake or whatever we had to give or to spare, there was a good many came around in those times.

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Did they ever stay in the area for any length of time or did they just stop for a meal and keep on going?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: They would just stop and if you'd give them something to eat they would thank you for it and then they'd go. There was a, a certain, a certain Mr. Fisher that came around every year and he just had several places where he stopped that writing, thats what he made. Ah they made writing or paper, paper rocks or leather rocks, or . . .

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Like, like comb racks and things like that?

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab:
Yes, comb racks. They carried the wood along with them. They'd have ah, ah,
ah, bundle that they would carry you know and they would ask you for, oh for this old man that made these paper rocks he would ask for you to give him a piece of bacon or a couple potatoes he would make a fire out and eat roast potatoes in the ashes he said and oh sometimes he wanted sauerkraut or something that he could boil out in the woods. He never wanted to, to,to come in the house and eat a meal with us he always wanted something to take along out and he would, he would cook for himself outside. (laughs)

sp.speaker: Joan:
sp.ab: Then he'd pay you by making the comb rack.

sp.speaker: Ada:
sp.ab: Yes he'd, he would, yes he would have his wood along and, and if you would give him enough why he would make you a comb rack or a paper rack or... and they, they were nice we, I know a lot of people that have them and I have one now and there. different people that said they wished they could get one like it. They're old you know, my that was way back. And it must have been a hundred years ago because it, it, my father-in-law had it and then Norman got it and now I have it yet. And then there was a, a, it was supposed to be a comb box, you could use it for a comb or for a paper rack and Connie has that. Oh she thought that was wonderful. She took that along and fixed it up to hang up. She liked antiques so much. There's nobody comes around you’ know, for years nobody's come around and asked for something to eat like use to but then people weren't, weren't kept like they are now and they didn't . . .
